title: Tar, Paper and the Fight on the Wall: the Painter Jaz from Buenos Aires to the Commissioned Barrio
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Workshop and the Opera House

stops.name: Buenos Aires, born into a house of painters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; MutualArt's index gives 1981, no month, day or birthplace within Argentina is documented anywhere reachable
stops.campa: A son is born in Buenos Aires to a family of artists, in a household where paint is furniture and improvisation is method. The address goes unrecorded; the household does not. He grows up watching people work on surfaces, and learns before he can name it that a surface is something a person takes in hand and changes. Nothing in the workshop points toward minotaurs or walls painted in road tar. What these years leave behind is a family trade and an address nobody wrote down. The tag JAZ does not exist yet.
suggested_refs: The unrecorded family workshop in Buenos Aires, his first studio
MutualArt artist index entry, 'Franco Fasoli, Argentinian, born 1981'
sources: MutualArt.com artist listing
streetartnews.net, 'Artist Retrospective: Franco Fasoli aka JAZ', 16 February 2022

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first walls
stops.date_confidence: contested; graffitimundo says mid 1990s, Fasoli's own 2011 interview says 1999, and neither source names a precise year
stops.campa: He goes into the street with paint before he is out of his teens, one of the first of a generation writing letters on Buenos Aires concrete when the city has no market for the work and nobody is photographing it. The sources disagree on the year: his own account puts the beginning at 1999, alongside Poeta, Caru, Nerf, Roma and Pastel; the graffiti chroniclers put it in the middle of the decade. Nothing survives of the earliest pieces, and no photograph fixes the year either way. He paints for several years before anyone thinks to keep a count.
stops.quote: recognized as one of the first major graffiti writers to begin painting in the streets of Buenos Aires in the mid 1990's
suggested_refs: The unlocated first pieces of the mid-1990s Buenos Aires writing scene
The peer group named by Fasoli: Poeta, Caru, Nerf, Roma, Pastel
sources: graffitimundo.com, artist profile 'Jaz'
Buenos Aires Street Art, 'All that Jaz and tango: Interview with street artist Franco Fasoli', 1 June 2011
brooklynstreetart.com, Franco Fasoli tag page

stops.name: Teatro Colon, the scenography years
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source gives a year for the Teatro Colon training, only that it happened
stops.campa: At the Instituto del Teatro Colon he studies scenography, the craft of building conviction at architectural scale for an audience that will never touch the set. He learns backdrop, painted depth, the trick of a surface meant to be read once from thirty meters and believed. Painting itself he takes elsewhere, from Jose Marchi, Nahuel Vecino and Diana Aisemberg. In the same years he and the other writers turn an idea over in conversation: that fileteado, the porteno sign tradition of scroll and shadow, could be crossed with graffiti lettering.
stops.quote: the idea of mixing the theme of fileteado with graffitis
stops.quote_source: Franco Fasoli, in Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011
suggested_refs: The Instituto Superior de Arte of the Teatro Colon, where he trained in scenography
The fileteado porteno sign-painting tradition of Buenos Aires
sources: graffitimundo.com, artist profile 'Jaz'
Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011

stops.name: Barcelona, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: approximate; sources date the trip only as a visit in early adulthood, the 2003-2004 window is an estimate
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic for the first time and finds Barcelona already thick with the public art he has only seen photographed: stencils and throw-ups on facades the city argues about rather than prosecutes. He walks the old quarter reading walls the way other travelers read guidebooks, and paints nothing while he is there. He names the trip later as the turn. After it, hip-hop lettering is one thing a wall can carry rather than the whole of the job, and Buenos Aires is one city on a map that has others on it.
suggested_refs: The Barri Gotic of Barcelona, walked as a young painter
graffitimundo's account of the Barcelona trip as the pivot toward public art
sources: graffitimundo.com, 'Jaz - new residence and global tour'
streetartnews.net, 'Artist Interview: Jaz', 23 June 2015

stops.name: Palermo Hollywood, the letters give way to figures
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, approximately; Fasoli dates the shift to around 2005
stops.campa: Around 2005 the letters give way to figures. He paints musicians, mostly, on walls in and around Palermo Hollywood, a barrio filling with recording studios and television crews while its side streets stay cheap enough to paint on. He will call the graffiti of these years naive, and mean it as description rather than apology: the drawing is still learning what it wants, the hand ahead of the argument. Musicians give him a reason to draw a body doing something, and from here the work is almost always a body doing something to another body.
stops.quote_source: Franco Fasoli on his 2005 street work, Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011
suggested_refs: The Palermo Hollywood walls of the mid-2000s musician portraits
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011

stops.name: Valparaiso, the musicians' wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; sources give January 2008 without a day
stops.campa: He paints musicians again, this time on a Valparaiso wall, alongside Fisek, Inti and Charquipunk, three painters of the Chilean port's own school. It is his first attested work outside Argentina. The mural is still standing when a visitor photographs it almost four years later, which in this trade counts as permanence. Valparaiso wears murals the way other cities wear advertising, layer over layer up the hills, and a piece that lasts four years there has survived a real test rather than an empty street.
suggested_refs: The Valparaiso musicians mural with Fisek, Inti and Charquipunk, photographed intact in October 2011
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'Jaz Franco Fasoli mural in Valparaiso, Chile', 22 October 2011
buenosairesstreetart.com profile page

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Aguante at Hollywood in Cambodia
stops.campa: He opens Aguante at the Hollywood in Cambodia gallery, a show about the barras bravas, the organized violence that runs alongside Argentine football like a second league. He abstracts the fighting into scenes, paints the known hooligans as portraits, and gives one room over to visitors, who are invited to add tattoo designs to the painted bodies. The devotion he is anatomizing is the one whose saint is Diego Maradona, a face Fasoli is credited with painting at mural scale elsewhere, though not in this room.
suggested_refs: The Hollywood in Cambodia gallery, Buenos Aires
The interactive tattoo room of the Aguante exhibition, August 2010
sources: graffitimundo.com, 'Aguante by Jaz @ HIC'

stops.name: Villa Crespo, the tussling torsos
stops.date_confidence: attested as the documentation date; the painting date is not separately recorded
stops.campa: On a Villa Crespo wall two torsos lock in a wrestler's hold, faceless, with no ground under them and no crowd around them. He is working now from lucha libre, from sumo, from the terraces, and from animals: donkeys first, then wolf-headed and lion-headed men. Animals suit him because they arrive with no attitude already attached, no politics a viewer has to agree with before looking. He says what drives him is the painting and not the concept. Neither torso is winning, and the wall gives a viewer no way to tell which one might.
stops.quote: the act of painting rather than an idea or a concept
stops.quote_source: Franco Fasoli, Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011
suggested_refs: The Villa Crespo wrestling-torso mural, documented 6 October 2011
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'Tussling torsos: new mural by Jaz in Buenos Aires', 6 October 2011
Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011

stops.name: Villa Crespo, bulls of mud, brick and coal
stops.campa: At a bus depot in Villa Crespo he paints two bulls locking horns, using mud, brick and coal picked up on the site itself. A week earlier the same found materials had gone onto a wall along Thames and Camargo. The method matters more than the beasts: no aerosol, no color chart, a mural made out of the ground it stands on, carrying the exact grey of the block it was scraped from. It is the start of the material habit that defines the next three years, tar and gasoline and whatever the site will surrender to a rag.
suggested_refs: The Villa Crespo bus depot bulls, painted in site-sourced mud, brick and coal, 14 January 2012
The companion mural at Thames and Camargo, early January 2012
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'New mural by Jaz in Villa Crespo', 15 January 2012

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Jaz plus Ever at the Oasis Clubhouse
stops.campa: He shows with Nicolas Romero, who paints as Ever and with whom he has shared a workshop, at the Oasis Clubhouse, presented by graffitimundo. The gallery notes what the two have in common: both began in letters, both abandoned them for figures, and the figures went in opposite directions. Ever went toward portraits and politics. Fasoli went toward beasts. They will keep painting together for years, on walls in more than one country, without either one converting the other to his own subject.
stops.quote: two of the leading artists to emerge from the Buenos Aires urban art scene
suggested_refs: The Oasis Clubhouse, Buenos Aires, venue of the 2012 Jaz + Ever exhibition
sources: graffitimundo.com, 'Jaz + Ever' exhibition announcement, 19 March 2012
Buenos Aires Street Art interview, 1 June 2011

stops.name: Villa Martelli, the sabre-toothed cats
stops.campa: In Villa Martelli he paints two smilodons, sabre-toothed cats ten thousand years extinct, and writes beside them that Jaz was here. The line is older than the mural and older than the commission, the first thing anybody who paints in a street has ever done: mark that a body stood at this exact spot and no other. He has spent fifteen years learning to paint animals that went extinct before there were walls, and he signs them with the sentence a child scratches into a school desk.
stops.quote_source: Text painted on the Villa Martelli mural, documented 22 August 2012
suggested_refs: The Villa Martelli smilodon mural, August 2012
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'New street art by Jaz in Buenos Aires', 22 August 2012

stops.name: Castillo and Fitz Roy, the depot wildcats
stops.campa: At a bus depot on the corner of Castillo and Fitz Roy he paints four wildcats and a rider on horseback, gaucho and folklore imagery at the scale of a city block. The sources cannot agree what barrio the corner sits in: one files it under Chacarita, another under Palermo. The same week he also paints at Tecnopolis, the state science and industry park on the northern edge of the city, which is a different kind of commission entirely. The cats come down over the wall in the same posture either way.
suggested_refs: The bus depot at Castillo and Fitz Roy, Buenos Aires, painted twice in ten days
The Tecnopolis mural of August 2012
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'New giant mural by Jaz in Chacarita', 27 August 2012
streetartnews.net, 'Jaz x Dotz New Mural In Buenos Aires', 3 September 2012

stops.name: Castillo and Fitz Roy, Los Guardianes with Dotz
stops.date_confidence: attested as the publication date of the completed wall
stops.campa: He returns to the same corner with Dotz, and together they raise six lions against one gigantic insect and call it Los Guardianes, the guardians. Scale favors the lions; the painting refuses to say who wins, catching the fight at its middle rather than its end. Two vocabularies share the plaster without merging, his tar-dark line against the other painter's own hand. Passersby stop for the insect before they count the lions. Nothing in the title says what the guardians are guarding, or from what.
stops.quote: six of Jaz's lions trying to fight off a gigantic insect painted by Dotz
stops.quote_source: streetartnews.net, 'Jaz x Dotz New Mural In Buenos Aires', 3 September 2012
suggested_refs: Los Guardianes, painted between Calle Fitz Roy and Calle Castillo
sources: streetartnews.net, 'Jaz x Dotz New Mural In Buenos Aires', 3 September 2012

stops.name: Santurce, San Juan, the walls that speak
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; posts on 10 and 14 October document work in progress and completed
stops.campa: For Los Muros Hablan he paints in Santurce, working bitumen into the wall until the mural looks watercolored rather than sprayed. The medium is road tar, gasoline, and a rag doing as much of the work as any brush. The result reads weather-stained on the day it is finished, a mural that arrives already looking as though it survived something. The festival puts Latin American and Caribbean painters on the same blocks, one wall at a time, and his piece takes its place among them without ceremony.
suggested_refs: The Los Muros Hablan festival walls of Santurce, October 2012
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural In Progress / Completed, San Juan', 10 and 14 October 2012

stops.name: Cerro Polanco, Valparaiso, painted in hours
stops.campa: He paints Cerro Polanco for the Polanco Graffestival, on a hill where houses climb over houses and no wall can be seen whole from any distance. The piece goes up in hours. There is no white space around it; the wall already carries other hands and his joins the pile. Valparaiso wears its murals as a second facade, and the arrangement is understood on all sides: whatever he leaves on this wall will in time be painted over by whoever arrives after him.
suggested_refs: The Polanco Graffestival walls of Cerro Polanco, Valparaiso
sources: streetartnews.net, 'Franco Fasoli JAZ New Street Art, Valparaiso', 19 November 2012

stops.name: Cordoba, beside Elian
stops.campa: In Cordoba he paints beside Elian, his tar figuration set against the other painter's geometric abstraction, the wall splitting visibly into two hands. Neither yields ground. It is his standing method by now: paint beside, never over, and let a surface record two decisions instead of forcing one. Cordoba's scene is younger and more thinly documented than the capital's, filed in festival photographs rather than gallery records. He will come back to this city in four years through a museum door, with the province's own history as his subject.
suggested_refs: The Cordoba collaboration wall with Elian, November 2012
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ x Elian New Mural In Cordoba', 22 November 2012

stops.name: Johannesburg, the last day of the year
stops.campa: He ends the year in Johannesburg, painting on its final day for the Acrylic Walls project. The grammar is the one he has been building for years: two forces meeting at the center line of the wall. The city has spent two decades treating murals as public argument and absorbs the piece without comment. He leaves almost no words about the visit. Within two weeks he will be painting at the other end of the country, and the trip will be misfiled in later accounts as one year's work when it straddles the turn of two.
suggested_refs: The Acrylic Walls project, Johannesburg, 31 December 2012
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural for Acrylic Walls, Johannesburg', 31 December 2012
Brooklyn Street Art, aggregated profile

stops.name: Woodstock, Cape Town, a corner mid-conversion
stops.campa: On the corner of Sussex and Wright in Woodstock he paints large in bitumen. Three days later he shows two indoor pieces at the Woodstock Exchange on Albert Road, the same technique under a roof, read at arm's length instead of across a street. The neighborhood is mid-conversion, warehouses turning from industry into design studios, walls turning from surface into asset. The mural makes no comment on any of this. It stands on a corner that will not look like this for much longer.
suggested_refs: The bitumen mural at Sussex and Wright Street, Woodstock
The two indoor pieces at the Woodstock Exchange, 66-68 Albert Road
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural In Cape Town, South Africa', 11 January 2013
streetartnews.net, 'JAZ Indoor Pieces, Woodstock Exchange, Cape Town', 14 January 2013

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Difusion with Ever
stops.campa: Back in Buenos Aires he and Ever paint a wall titled Difusion, propaganda, his tar figures beside a portrait of Mao Zedong in Ever's hand. Political portraiture is not his register; it is his friend's. The collaboration reads as a loan of vocabulary in both directions, made under a title that names the machinery rather than the man: how an image travels, who reproduces it, what survives the reproduction. The finished wall settles nothing about Mao. It says a great deal about circulation.
suggested_refs: Difusion, the Buenos Aires collaboration wall with Ever, March 2013
sources: streetartnews.net, 'Jaz x Ever New Mural In Buenos Aires', 29 March 2013

stops.name: Antwerp, a solo show at Artifex
stops.campa: He opens a solo show at Artifex Gallery in Antwerp and paints an indoor piece for it, moving bitumen from exterior brick to gallery wall without visible friction. This month alone takes him through Belgium, France, Austria and Germany; the European gallery circuit has found him and the festival circuit has not let go. What the Antwerp show actually contained is thinly recorded. The press covers the walls and not the rooms, which is one way this trade loses its own history while it is still being made.
suggested_refs: Artifex Gallery, Antwerp, site of the 2013 solo exhibition
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural In Antwerp, Belgium', 8 May 2013
Brooklyn Street Art, aggregated profile

stops.name: Vienna, Cult to the Character
stops.date_confidence: attested; two posts date the street piece and the gallery preparation to 20 and 22 May 2013
stops.campa: In Vienna he paints in the street and then prepares the material for his solo show Cult to the Character at Inoperable Gallery, two stages within walking distance in a single week. The title could stand over most of his output: masked wrestlers and hybrids treated less as characters than as objects of devotion, painted over and over. The week produces a wall for anyone who walks past it and a room for whoever comes through the gallery door, and the two audiences will not see each other's version of the work.
suggested_refs: Inoperable Gallery, Burggasse 21, Vienna, venue of Cult to the Character
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural In Vienna, Austria, Parts I and II', 20 and 22 May 2013

stops.name: Kadikoy, Istanbul, the Asian shore
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; posts on 16 and 19 June cover the wall in progress and completed
stops.campa: For Mural-IST he paints at Kadikoy on Istanbul's Asian shore, bitumen across a wall large enough to hold the collision he keeps returning to: two forces, one center line. The city leaves a second trace on him. An Ottoman warrior on horseback follows him home and resurfaces months later as a hand-painted screenprint, the visit converted from wall to paper once the tar has dried and the festival crews have moved along to the next block of the neighborhood.
suggested_refs: The Mural-IST festival wall at Kadikoy, June 2013
The Ottoman horseman screenprint made after the Istanbul visit
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural In Progress / Completed, Istanbul', 16 and 19 June 2013

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the wall shared with Hyuro
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; posts of 24 and 28 July cover the work
stops.campa: He paints in Buenos Aires with Hyuro, whose faceless elongated women meet his hybrids on shared plaster. She has worked across Argentina for years and he is home; the wall belongs to both of them and to neither one alone. Neither language translates into the other, and neither painter tries to make it. He has worked this way with Ever, with Dotz, with Elian, and he will go on working this way through the decade: two hands on one surface, each of them finishing its own sentence.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires collaboration wall with Hyuro, July 2013
sources: streetartnews.net, 'Jaz x Hyuro New Mural In Buenos Aires', 24 and 28 July 2013

stops.name: Atlanta, North Against South
stops.date_confidence: attested; posts of 12 and 15 August 2013 cover the wall
stops.campa: At the Living Walls Conference he paints North Against South in two days and meets, on adjoining scaffolding, painters he has known only through documentation: Escif, Sam3, Blu. He calls Atlanta his first international festival invitation, though Cape Town and Johannesburg are already months behind him; the contradiction stands in his own account and is left standing. The title carries an American sectional weight the piece may not intend. He has been painting one force against another since the barras, and Atlanta only supplies the phrase for it.
suggested_refs: North Against South, Living Walls Conference, Atlanta, August 2013
sources: streetartnews.net, 'Artist Interview: Jaz', 23 June 2015
streetartnews.net, North Against South posts, 12 and 15 August 2013

stops.name: Queretaro, No Correr
stops.campa: For the Board Dripper festival he paints No Correr, do not run, in Queretaro, part of what he is calling the Hooligan series: figures drawn out of stadium crowds rather than out of myth or the animal register. The title reads as instruction or as warning depending on who is being addressed, the crowd or the person standing in front of it. The colonial center takes on one more layer. Its baroque facades have watched several centuries of flight and confrontation without a festival ever naming either one.
suggested_refs: No Correr, Board Dripper festival, Queretaro, September 2013
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural No Correr, Queretaro', 7 September 2013

stops.name: Wynwood, Miami, the cats come down on the city
stops.campa: During Art Basel week he paints wildcats descending on Wynwood, the visiting artists rendered as predators arriving in a city that invited them. It takes three days, an extension pole and a paintbrush. He works alongside other painters out of Buenos Aires: Sonni, Magda Love, Amor, Pelos de Plumas, and the writer Nase. Wynwood is by now an outdoor museum built on purpose for the collectors who arrive each winter, and its wall inventory turns over faster than almost anywhere he paints. The cats will not outlast the decade.
suggested_refs: The Wynwood Walls mural of December 2013
The Argentine contingent at Art Basel Miami 2013: Sonni, Magda Love, Amor, Pelos de Plumas, Nase
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'Argentine street artists at Wynwood Walls in Miami', 8 December 2013
streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural Miami, Wynwood', 9 December 2013

stops.name: Ushuaia, the painted hull
stops.campa: At the bottom of the continent, in Ushuaia, he and Seth Globepainter paint an abandoned boat. There is no wall worth the journey, so the hull will do, retired from use before either painter touched it. It is the strangest support in his record and the most literal: a vessel that carried people, painted by two men who spend their working lives being carried. The town sells itself as the southernmost city on earth and collects superlatives the way other places collect anniversaries. Briefly it has a painted boat.
suggested_refs: The abandoned boat at Ushuaia painted with Seth Globepainter, January 2014
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ x Seth Globepainter, Ushuaia', 27 January 2014

stops.name: Perth, Moving Forward
stops.date_confidence: attested; posts of 7 and 17 April 2014 cover roughly ten days of work
stops.campa: For the Form public art festival he paints Moving Forward over roughly ten days in central Perth, where commissioned murals are being used as municipal policy, blank walls handed to international painters as a stated strategy for remaking a downtown's image. The title reads almost as civic slogan, which may be the joke or may be the brief. Weeks later he is on the far coast, painting Melbourne laneways in tar and gasoline, where the walls turn over so fast that nobody records what he left behind.
suggested_refs: Moving Forward, Form Public Art Festival, Perth, April 2014
The Melbourne laneway pieces of late April 2014
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural Moving Forward, Perth', 7 and 17 April 2014
streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Street Pieces, Melbourne', 26 April 2014

stops.name: Erriadh, Djerba, four conquests on one wall
stops.campa: At Djerbahood, in the island village of Erriadh, he paints the civilisations that conquered the country in succession: Greeks, Romans, Vandals, Arabs, stacked onto a single wall. The festival is turning an entire village into an open-air museum, with more than a hundred painters eventually contributing, most of them chosen for spectacle. His piece is doing history instead. The island's communities have coexisted here for centuries, and the wall gestures at the layering without resolving it into one story with one winner.
stops.quote: four of the civilisations that conquered Tunisia, the Greeks, the Romans, the Vandals and the Arabs
stops.quote_source: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural, Djerba, Tunisia', 8 August 2014
suggested_refs: The Djerbahood open-air museum at Erriadh, Djerba
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural, Djerbahood, Djerba', 8 August 2014

stops.name: Barracas, the bridge painted in club colors
stops.campa: Under the Puente Bosch railway bridge in Barracas he paints tattooed half-men and half-beasts, with Pastel adding the plant life around them. The palette is lifted from the strips of the two local clubs, Deportivo Barracas and Barracas Central, so the barrio recognizes its own colors before it recognizes the figures. It is their first mural together since Saavedra in 2011. He is sharing a Villa Crespo studio with Pastel by now and describing himself plainly as middle class and university educated, which in this trade is a confession.
suggested_refs: The mural beneath the Puente Bosch railway bridge, Barracas, November 2014
The shared Villa Crespo studio of Fasoli and Pastel
sources: Buenos Aires Street Art, 'Jaz and Pastel new mural in Barracas', 1 November 2014
graffitimundo.com, 'Interview: Jaz and Pastel', 2015

stops.name: Ciudad Juarez, a counter-claim on a wall
stops.campa: He paints in Ciudad Juarez for the Color Walk festival, framed by its organizers as urban restoration, in a city whose name has for years been shorthand in every foreign newspaper for the drug war. The mural does not address the violence; festival murals rarely do. It works instead as a counter-claim: the city contains blocks willing to be painted and photographed for reasons unrelated to what the border is famous for, and the people organizing the festival live on them.
suggested_refs: The Color Walk festival walls of Ciudad Juarez, November 2014
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural, Ciudad Juarez', 19 November 2014

stops.name: Rio San Juan, the technique changing hands
stops.campa: For ArteSano he paints in Rio San Juan on the Dominican north coast, a fishing town whose economy runs on tourism and agriculture and not at all on art. He has come from a Miami residency where he was working out the technique he will lean on hard through the following year: cut colored paper, pasted and layered onto the wall before any paint arrives, composition assembled the way a stage set is assembled. Whether the Rio San Juan wall used it is not recorded by anyone who was there.
suggested_refs: The ArteSano street art festival, Rio San Juan, December 2014
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ creates new mural in Rio San Juan', 21 December 2014
streetartnews.net, 'Artist Interview: Jaz', 23 June 2015

stops.name: Rabat, The Shoe Thief
stops.date_confidence: attested; the festival wall is reported on 20 and 21 May 2015
stops.campa: At the Jidar festival in Rabat he paints The Shoe Thief in layered colored paper, the collage technique now fully his own, carried across murals and gallery pieces alike. The mural is described as an inquiry into tension, violence and tribal identity, which is a fair description of everything he has painted since the barras. Shadows enter the composition, figures not fully present, combatants made partly out of absence. The Moroccan capital is investing in murals as diplomacy and takes the fight scene without flinching.
suggested_refs: The Shoe Thief, Jidar Toiles de Rue festival, Rabat, May 2015
sources: graffitimundo.com, 'Jaz in Morocco', 20 May 2015
streetartnews.net, 'JAZ New Mural, Rabat Jidar Festival', 21 May 2015

stops.name: Cozumel, Eat This
stops.campa: For SeaWalls he paints Eat This on Cozumel, a shark, and the festival states the argument plainly: the mural warns against harvesting shark fins for soup. Advocacy is not his usual register; he takes the brief anyway. The festival exists to turn muralism into marine campaigning, dozens of painters working coastal towns to put reef health and fishing pressure on a wall where a diver walking down to the boat will see it. He is spending more than half of each year on the road by now.
stops.quote: warns us against harvesting sharks fins for soup
stops.quote_source: streetartnews.net, 'SeaWalls 15: Eat This, new mural by JAZ', July 2015
suggested_refs: Eat This, SeaWalls / PangeaSeed festival, Cozumel, July 2015
sources: streetartnews.net, 'SeaWalls 15: JAZ in Cozumel', 21 and 27 July 2015
graffitimundo.com, 'Jaz - new residence and global tour'

stops.name: Largo do Arouche, Sao Paulo, ten days beside Harrington
stops.campa: In the Largo do Arouche he paints for ten days beside Conor Harrington, whose brawling figures in historical dress meet his masked hybrids on the same square. Ten days is long by festival standards, long enough for two visual languages to argue rather than merely coexist. Sao Paulo has one of the densest mural scenes anywhere, tolerated and then commissioned after years of prosecuting pichacao as a crime. The flower market goes on selling underneath them while the two of them work above it.
suggested_refs: The Largo do Arouche wall shared with Conor Harrington, October 2015
sources: streetartnews.net, 'JAZ x Conor Harrington, Largo do Arouche, Sao Paulo', 30 October 2015

stops.name: Madrid, The Rapture
stops.campa: He closes the year in Madrid with The Rapture, a diptych of half-human half-animal figures locked in combat, the minotaur surfacing as his clearest classical reference yet: the man-bull of the labyrinth taken out of the myth cycle and put onto two separate surfaces. The split forces a viewer to walk between them to complete the fight. Twelve months have carried him from Rabat to Cozumel to Sao Paulo, and Madrid arrives as the European clasp on a year spent almost entirely somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The Rapture, diptych mural, Madrid, December 2015
sources: streetartnews.net, 'The Rapture, new mural by Jaz in Madrid', 30 December 2015

stops.name: Ostend, painting after Ensor
stops.campa: For the Crystal Ship he paints in Ostend, working from James Ensor, the town's own painter of grotesque masked crowds and the first name anybody here says. The reference is unusually direct for him, a named art-historical source rather than myth or sport in the abstract. The North Sea light is grey and the palette follows it, muted, closer to Ensor's own than to the tar-black contrast he carried through the tropics. Masks meeting masks on the same coast, a century between the two hands.

stops.name: Cordoba, First free territory of America
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exhibition ran 19 May to 28 July 2016
stops.campa: At the Museo Provincial de Bellas Artes Emilio Caraffa his piece First free territory of America enters Pioneers of Trip to Nowhere, an exhibition on the identity and the violence of Cordoba's provincial history. He does not make it alone. He works first with residents of the Alberdi neighborhood on the development of the piece and only then finishes the composition by himself, an honest division of labor and an unusual one to put in writing. A street work has come indoors and brought its street in with it.

stops.name: Alberdi, the work goes back to the street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the exhibition's closing date; the reinstallation is dated only as after the close
stops.campa: When the exhibition closes, the work does not go into storage and does not go into a collection. It goes back to Alberdi, reinstalled at the place in the neighborhood it came out of, among the people who helped develop it. The museum was the detour. Twenty years after he started painting walls without asking, the traffic runs the other way for once: out of the institution and back into the barrio, a piece borrowed by a province and returned to the block that lent it in the first place.

stops.name: Kyiv, the wall at Gymnasium 267
stops.date_confidence: attested as the publication date; the painting took seven days
stops.campa: At Gymnasium 267 on Verbytskoho Street, in a Soviet-built housing district on the left bank of the Dnipro, he spends seven days painting two symmetrical felines in a forest, communicating through the patterns on their skin. The commission is Mural Social Club's Back to School, and the audience is children who will walk past this wall every morning for years rather than tourists photographing it once. The fighting stops and the masks come off. The two animals are looking at each other, and at nothing else.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, TODO with Jorge Pomar
stops.campa: He paints in Buenos Aires again with Jorge Pomar, ten meters by three, and they call it TODO: everything. The color is vivid, with no trace of the tar monochrome of a decade before; collage came first, then color, and the black years are behind him. The city has spent much of the preceding year under one of the longest lockdowns anywhere on earth. A wall that says everything, painted in a season that offered very little, reads as a claim staked whether or not either painter set out to stake it.

stops.name: Trinitat Nova, Barcelona commissions him
stops.date_confidence: attested as the inauguration date; the reporting post is dated 5 August 2021
stops.campa: In Trinitat Nova, a Barcelona neighborhood built from the 1950s to house migrant labor and kept off every tourist map since, he paints for the TIME project with local residents and with students from the Catalan school of restoration and conservation. The imagery includes bulls, recalling the district's agricultural past. The organizers call the project a tool for social transformation through art. Some eighteen years after a young painter walked this city reading its facades, the city commissions him with public money.

stops.name: Basildon, a new town in Essex
stops.campa: For the Our Towns initiative he paints large in Basildon, a postwar English new town that appears on no international mural itinerary and has spent seventy years being mocked in the national press for the way it was planned. The funder is a creative people and places programme betting on culture as regeneration, and the wall is part of the bet. Twenty-five years earlier he was painting Buenos Aires concrete that nobody commissioned and nobody photographed. Here he arrives by invitation, with a budget and a lift.

stops.name: Ostend, the second Crystal Ship
stops.date_confidence: the retrospective is dated 16 February 2022; the second Ostend murals are listed for 2022 without a day or month
stops.campa: He returns to Ostend and the Crystal Ship six years after Ensor, one of the very few festivals in his record he has painted twice. The same year a retrospective runs under both his names, Franco Fasoli and JAZ, which is the shape the career has taken: the alias for the walls, the given name for the rooms, no visible anxiety about which of the two is the real one. He is roughly forty and still working. There is no grave to visit, and no legend has yet grown up around him without him.
